To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a supervised machine learning algorithm can be used to infer the existence and direction of causal links between two variables in Markov indistinuishable configurations with more than two variables, and that (2) this can be done with high accuracy, even if the number of variables is relatively large (n > 10).

1) supervised learning methods may extract causal information from asymmetric conditional (in)dependencies; 2) the causal information extracted by the method may be used to improve the accuracy of causal discovery algorithms; 3) causal information may be extracted even from n > 2 variable distributions.

(i) the asymmetry of conditional independence relations can be exploited to learn the causal structure in multivariate settings; (ii) this asymmetry can be captured by the use of the so-called conditional mutual information; (iii) the asymmetry in the conditional mutual information is a function of the causal structure and can therefore be used as a supervised learning target to infer the causal structure of a system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of inferring causation from statistical dependency.
the question of whether the asymmetry of the (in)dependence structure of a distribution can be used to infer causality.

the following question: is there a way to infer the existence and directionality of causal links in multivariate distributions by exploiting the asymmetry of conditional (in) dependence relations between the variables in the Markov blanket of a pair of variables causally related?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in general, there is no simple relation between the existence of a causal relationship and the existence of a statistical dependency, and that the relation between the two notions is not only a matter of directionality but also of strength and of the number of involved variables.
the existence of causal relationships can be inferred with a good accuracy even in the presence of Markov indistinguishability.
the machine learning approach to causal discovery is able to detect causal relations even in the presence of hidden confounders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the asymmetries of some conditional independence relations are sufficient for inferring the causal directionality of the causal links between pairs of variables.

the existence of causal relations can be inferred from the asymmetries of the conditional independences among variables, and the machine learning approach proposed here can successfully exploit this fact.
, in multivariate settings, a directed causal link can be inferred from the asymmetry of conditional independence relations between the members belonging to the Markov blankets.
The main takeaway from our work is that
supervised learning techniques can be successfully used to infer causal information from multivariate data.
supervised learning can be used to extract information from the data that cannot be extracted by statistical methods.
, even if the Markov blanket of two causally connected variables may be symmetric, there may still be some asymmetries that can be exploited to detect the causal direction.
